sec.title: Background
sec.p: Cardiovascular diseases, overweight, type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease increase the risk of cardiovascular events.

Glucagon-like peptide-1 analogues are recommended by the European Society of Cardiology and the American College of Cardiology to lower the risk of death and progression of cardiovascular disease in patients with cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes. Semaglutide, tirzepatide and liraglutide are approved by the US Food and Drug Administration and the European Medicines Agency for the treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus and overweight. CagriSema is currently not approved, but several phase III trials are ongoing.

No previous systematic review has investigated the effects of semaglutide, tirzepatide, CagriSema and liraglutide, which may not be disease-specific, on hard binary outcomes for all trial populations at increased risk of cardiovascular events.

sec.title: Methods and analyses
sec.p: We will conduct a systematic review and search major medical databases (Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Medical Literature Analysis and Retrieval System Online, Excerpta Medica database, Latin American and Caribbean Health Sciences Literature, Science Citation Index Expanded, Conference Proceedings Citation Index—Science) and clinical trial registries from their inception and onwards to identify relevant randomised trials. We expect to perform the literature search in December 2025. Two review authors will independently extract data and assess the risk of bias. We will include randomised trials assessing the effects of semaglutide, tirzepatide, CagriSema and/or liraglutide in participants with an increased risk of cardiovascular events. The primary outcome will be all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes will be myocardial infarction, stroke and all-cause hospitalisation. Data will be synthesised by aggregate data meta-analyses, Trial Sequential Analyses and network meta-analysis, risk of bias will be assessed with Cochrane Risk of Bias tool V. 2, and the certainty of the evidence will be assessed by Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluations and the Confidence in Network Meta-Analysis approach.

sec.title: Ethics and dissemination
sec.p: This protocol does not present any results. Findings of this systematic review will be published in international peer-reviewed scientific journals.

caption.title: STRENGTHS AND LIMITATIONS OF THIS STUDY

list-item.p: We will assess hard binary outcomes with unquestionable patient importance.

The involvement of two independent investigators in literature screening, data extraction, risk-of-bias assessments and Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluations evaluations strengthens the credibility of the review.
Meta-analysing all trial populations at increased risk of cardiovascular events increases the statistical power.

We will address the risks of both random and systematic errors by employing a predefined, detailed methodology aligned with the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions, risk-of-bias assessments using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool V.2, Trial Sequential Analysis and a systematic assessment to determine whether the thresholds for statistical and clinical significance are crossed.
Including different types of participants at increased risk of cardiovascular events may potentially result in statistical heterogeneity.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: People with cardiovascular diseases, obesity, overweight with weight-related comorbidities (eg, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia or sleep apnoea syndrome), type 2 diabetes, metabolic-associated steatohepatitis or chronic kidney disease are at increased risk of developing microvascular and macrovascular disease (eg, atherosclerosis), potentially leading to cardiovascular events such as myocardial infarction, stroke or death.1,4 Cardiovascular diseases are the leading cause of death globally, accounting for an estimated 17.9 million deaths annually.5 Additionally, the prevalence of type 2 diabetes and obesity continues to rise worldwide.6 7

Glucagon-like peptide-1 analogues (GLP-1 RAs) are a relatively new class of drugs that mimic the effects of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), an enteroendocrine hormone produced in the small intestine.8 9 GLP-1 increases the glucose-dependent insulin secretion, slows gastric emptying and enhances satiety.9 Consequently, treatment with GLP-1 RAs results in supraphysiologic effects of GLP-1, contributing to improved glycaemic control and weight loss.9

Semaglutide and liraglutide are both GLP-1 RAs, and tirzepatide is a combined GLP-1 RA and glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide analogue.10,12 CagriSema is a combined GLP-1 RA (semaglutide) and amylin analogue (cagrilintide).13 GLP-1 RAs are recommended by the European Society of Cardiology14 and the American College of Cardiology15 as first-line therapy to lower the risk of death and progression of cardiovascular disease in patients with cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes. Semaglutide, tirzepatide and liraglutide are approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and European Medicines Agency (EMA) for the treatment of type 2 diabetes, obesity (body mass index (BMI) of at least 30 kg/m2) or overweight (BMI of at least 27 kg/m2) with at least one weight-related comorbidity (eg, hypertension, dyslipidaemia or sleep apnoea).16,26 By November 2025, CagriSema was not approved by either the FDA or the EMA, but several phase III trials have been published or are currently ongoing.27,32

sec.title: Previous evidence
sec.p: Several previous systematic reviews with network meta-analysis have investigated different GLP-1 RAs on glycaemic control and weight loss in participants with either type 2 diabetes or overweight.33,36 A living systematic review with network meta-analysis investigated different treatments for type 2 diabetes, including GLP-1 RAs.37 It found that GLP-1 RA, as a drug group, reduced the risk of all-cause death (risk ratio (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.82 to 0.92), non-fatal myocardial infarction (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.85 to 0.98) and non-fatal stroke (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.79 to 0.96) in participants with type 2 diabetes. However, several important trials have been published since that review, and it did not encompass all participants at increased risk of cardiovascular events. In addition, the authors did not employ Trial Sequential Analysis.

A systematic review with network meta-analysis from 2024 showed that treatment with semaglutide, tirzepatide and liraglutide reduced HbA1c and body weight in participants with type 2 diabetes compared with placebo, with tirzepatide being the most effective among these three agents.38

A systematic review with network meta-analysis from 2020 investigated the cardiovascular safety and mortality in participants with type 2 diabetes treated with GLP-1 RAs, based on cardiovascular outcome trials.39 The review showed that semaglutide was most effective in reducing major cardiovascular events, cardiovascular death and death from any cause.39 However, it did not include tirzepatide and CagriSema.

sec.title: Why is this review important?
sec.p: No previous systematic review with network meta-analysis and Trial Sequential Analysis has investigated the effects of semaglutide, tirzepatide, CagriSema and liraglutide—which may not be disease-specific—on hard binary outcomes for all assessed trial populations at increased risk of cardiovascular events. We have chosen these four drugs because semaglutide, tirzepatide and liraglutide are the only GLP-1 RAs approved by the FDA and EMA for the treatment of both type 2 diabetes mellitus and obesity.16,26 CagriSema is included in this review because it contains semaglutide as an active component, is currently tested in participants with type 2 diabetes mellitus or obesity in phase III trials, and is expected to be branded and approved as both an antidiabetic and antiobesity drug.28 32

sec.title: Methods and analyses
sec.p: The methods section is based on our previous systematic review protocol.40 In short, the protocol is reported in accordance with the reporting guideline provided in the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis Protocols (PRISMA-P) statement41 42 and is registered in the PROSPERO database (CRD42024623312). The protocol design was based on guidance from the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions.43

sec.title: Criteria for considering studies for this review
Types of trials
sec.p: We will include randomised clinical trials, irrespective of publication status, publication year and language. We will not include cluster-randomised studies, quasi-randomised studies (ie, trials with inappropriate allocation strategies for interventions),43 non-randomised studies (eg case–control studies) or observational studies.

sec.title: Types of participants
sec.p: Participants eligible for inclusion are adults at increased risk of cardiovascular events, as defined by the trialists, treated with semaglutide, tirzepatide, CagriSema or liraglutide.

If a trial did not explicitly define participants as being at increased risk of cardiovascular events, we will consider them to be at increased risk if they have any of the following: established cardiovascular disease, overweight with weight-related comorbidities, obesity, heart failure, diabetes mellitus, metabolic-associated steatohepatitis, hypertension or chronic kidney disease.

sec.title: Types of interventions
sec.p: We will accept all dosages of semaglutide, tirzepatide, CagriSema and liraglutide as experimental interventions. We will, as control interventions, accept semaglutide, tirzepatide, CagriSema, liraglutide, placebo, ‘active’ placebo or ‘no intervention’.

sec.title: Cointerventions
sec.p: We will accept any cointervention if it is intended to be delivered similarly in the intervention and control groups.

sec.title: Outcome measures
sec.p: The trial will be excluded if it does not report any of our outcomes.

sec.title: Primary outcome
sec.p: All-cause mortality.

list-item.p: Myocardial infarction (as defined by trialists).
Stroke (as defined by trialists).
All-cause hospitalisation.
Cardiovascular mortality (as defined by trialists).
Hospitalisation for cardiovascular reasons (as defined by trialists), for example, ‘heart failure requiring hospitalisation’ and ‘unstable angina requiring hospitalisation’.

sec.title: Assessment time points
sec.p: We will assess all outcomes at maximum follow-up.

sec.title: Search methods for the identification of studies
Electronic searches
sec.p: We will search Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Medical Literature Analysis and Retrieval System Online (MEDLINE) (MEDLINE Ovid), Excerpta Medica database (EMBASE) (Embase Ovid), Latin American and Caribbean Health Sciences Literature (VHL Regional Portal), Science Citation Index Expanded (Web of Science), Conference Proceedings Citation Index—Science (Web of Science) to identify relevant trials. We will search all databases from their inception to the present. Trials will be included irrespective of language, publication status, publication year and publication type. For a detailed search strategy for all electronic searches, see online supplemental material. We expect to conduct the literature search in December 2025.

sec.title: Searching other resources
sec.p: The reference lists of relevant trial publications will be checked for any unidentified randomised clinical trials. To identify unpublished trials, we will search clinical trial registries (eg, clinicaltrials.gov, clinicaltrialregister.eu, who.int/ictrp, chictr.org.cn) worldwide.

We will also include unpublished trials if we identify these and assess relevant retraction statements and errata for included trials. We will also try to obtain clinical study reports from regulatory authorities, as these are known to be more transparent in reporting adverse events.44,49 We will also search preprint servers (bioRxiv, medRxiv, Open Science Format) for unpublished trials.

sec.title: Data collection
sec.p: We will report the review as recommended by the PRISMA statement extension for systematic reviews incorporating network meta-analysis.50 Analyses will be performed using Stata 18 (StataCorp LLC, College Station, Texas)51 and Trial Sequential Analysis.52 53

sec.title: Selection of randomised clinical trials
sec.p: Two review authors will independently screen titles and abstracts. We will retrieve all relevant full-text study reports/publications, and two review authors will independently screen the full texts and will record reasons for excluding ineligible studies. The same two review authors will resolve disagreements through discussion, or if required, they will consult a third author (JCJ).

sec.title: Data extraction and management
sec.p: Two review authors will independently extract data from included trials in a predefined form. Disagreements will be resolved by discussion with a third author (JCJ). The two review authors will assess duplicate publications and companion papers of a trial together to evaluate all available data simultaneously (maximise data extraction, correct bias assessment). Each trial will be named after the first author and year of the primary publication, and all secondary publications will be classified under that name. We will contact the trial authors by email to specify any missing data, which may not be reported sufficiently or at all in the publication.
For trials that include more than one dose arm of the same drug, we will extract the data using two approaches:

list-item.p: Each dose arm will be extracted as an independent comparison. To avoid double-counting participants from the shared comparator group, the comparator group will be split across the dose arms following Cochrane recommendations.43 This approach allows us to conduct subgroup analyses based on treatment dose.

All dose arms will be pooled into a single intervention group and compared with the intact, non-split comparator group. This combined dataset will be used for the pairwise meta-analyses, Trial Sequential Analyses and network meta-analyses. This allows for comparison only at the treatment level in the network meta-analyses, as dose effects are not the primary comparison of interest in this review.43 54

sec.title: Trial characteristics
sec.p: We will extract the following data: bias risk components (as defined below), trial design (parallel, factorial or crossover), number of intervention groups, length of follow-up, estimation of sample size, and inclusion and exclusion criteria.

sec.title: Participant characteristics
sec.p: We will extract the following data: number of randomised participants, number of analysed participants, number of participants lost to follow-up/withdrawals/crossover, age range (mean or median), sex ratio, primary diagnosis (eg, type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity, hypertension, chronic kidney disease), HbA1c (mean and SD) and BMI (mean and SD).

sec.title: Experimental intervention characteristics
sec.p: We will extract the following data: administration form (oral or subcutaneous) and dosage of semaglutide, tirzepatide, CagriSema and liraglutide, and length of treatment period.

sec.title: Control intervention characteristics
sec.p: We will extract the following data: type of control (semaglutide, tirzepatide, CagriSema, liraglutide, placebo, ‘active’ placebo or no intervention), dosage and length of treatment period.

sec.title: Outcomes
sec.p: All outcomes listed above will be extracted from each randomised clinical trial. For each outcome, we will identify if there are deviations from intended interventions, if outcomes are missing, inappropriately measured or selectively reported according to the criteria described later in the ‘deviation from intended interventions’ bias domain, ‘missing outcome data’ bias domain, the ‘risk of bias in measurement of the outcome’ bias domain and the ‘risk of bias in selection of the reported result’ bias domain.

sec.title: Notes
sec.p: We will search for information regarding industry funding of either personal or academic activities for each trial author. We will judge a publication at high risk of for-profit bias if a trial is sponsored by the industry or if just one author has affiliation to the industry.55 We will note in the ‘Characteristics of included trials’ table if outcome data were not reported in a usable way. Disagreements will be resolved through discussion, or if required, we will consult with a third author (JCJ).

sec.title: Assessment of risk of bias in the included trials
sec.p: Our bias risk assessment will be based on the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool – V.2 as recommended in the Cochrane Handbook of Systematic Reviews of Interventions.43 We will evaluate the methodology with respect to the following bias domains:

list-item.p: Bias arising from the randomisation process.
Bias due to deviation from intended interventions (effect of assignment to intervention).
Bias due to missing outcome data.
Bias in measurement of outcomes.
Bias arising from selective reporting of results.
Overall assessment of risk of bias.

sec.p: We will assess the domains ‘deviations from intended interventions’, ‘missing outcome data’, ‘risk of bias in measurement of the outcome’ and ‘risk of bias in selection of the reported result’ for each outcome result. Thus, we can assess the bias risk for each outcome assessed in addition to each trial. The overall risk of bias of a result or trial will be judged to be low if all domains are assessed at low risk of bias. If one or more domains are assessed as having some concerns or high risk of bias, the overall risk of bias will be assessed as high. Our primary conclusions will be based on the results of our primary outcome results at overall low risk of bias. Both our primary and secondary conclusions will be presented in the summary of findings tables.

sec.title: Differences between the protocol and the review
sec.p: We will conduct the review according to this published protocol and report any deviations from it in the ‘Differences between the protocol and the review’ section of the systematic review.

sec.title: Dichotomous outcomes
sec.p: We will calculate RRs with 95% CI for dichotomous outcomes, as well as the Trial Sequential Analysis-adjusted CIs (see below).

sec.title: Dealing with missing data
sec.p: We will use intention-to-treat data if provided by the trialists.56 We will, as the first option, contact all trial authors to obtain any relevant missing data (ie, for data extraction and for assessment of risk of bias, as specified above).

sec.title: Dichotomous outcomes
sec.p: We will not impute missing values for any outcomes in our primary analysis. We will impute data in our sensitivity analyses (see below).

sec.title: Assessment of heterogeneity
sec.p: We will primarily visually investigate forest plots for signs of heterogeneity. We will then assess the presence of statistical heterogeneity using I2 statistic (ie, the percentage of total variation across trials apart from random variation, with 0% indicating no observed heterogeneity and increasing percentages indicating increasing heterogeneity)43 57 58 and restricted maximum likelihood method to estimate the heterogeneity variance.59 60 We will only conclude that the heterogeneity is high if the between trial variance translates to differences important to patients (based on the effect sizes defined in the Trial Sequential Analyses; see below). We will investigate heterogeneity through subgroup analyses (see ‘Subgroup analyses and integration of heterogeneity’ section). We may ultimately decide that a meta-analysis should be avoided if heterogeneity is high.43

sec.title: Assessment of reporting biases
sec.p: We will use a funnel plot to assess reporting bias if 10 or more trials are included.43 We will visually inspect funnel plots to assess the risk of bias. We are aware of the limitations of a funnel plot (ie, a funnel plot assesses small study bias).43 From this information, we will assess possible reporting bias. For dichotomous outcomes, we will test asymmetry with the Harbord test61 if τ2 is <0.1 and with the Rücker test if τ2 is >0.1.43

sec.title: Unit of analysis issues
sec.p: We will only include randomised clinical trials. For trials using crossover design, only data from the first period will be included,43 62 so there will be no unit of analysis issues.
All identified pairwise comparisons will be compared using meta-analyses, Trial Sequential Analyses, and subgroup and sensitivity analyses.

sec.title: Meta-analysis
sec.p: We will undertake the meta-analyses in accordance with the Cochrane Handbook of Systematic Reviews of Interventions,43 Keus et al63 and the eight-step assessment suggested by Jakobsen et al.64 We will use the statistical software Stata 18 to analyse data.51 We will assess the effects of our interventions using both a random-effects meta-analysis65 and a fixed-effect meta-analysis for each treatment comparison separately.66 We will primarily report the most conservative point estimate of the two (highest p value) and consider the less conservative result a sensitivity analysis.64

We will assess one primary outcome and, therefore, consider a p value of ≤0.05 as the threshold for statistical significance.64 We will investigate possible heterogeneity through subgroup analyses. We will use the eight-step procedure to assess if the thresholds for significance are crossed and assess the clinical significance of the review results.64 We will include only the relevant intervention groups (arms) where multiple trial arms are reported in a single trial. If two comparisons are combined in the same meta-analysis, we will split the control group to avoid double-counting.
Meta-analyses will not be performed when excessive heterogeneity is present (overall assessment by the author group).

sec.title: Trial Sequential Analysis
sec.p: We wish to control the risks of type 1 and 2 errors. We will, therefore, perform Trial Sequential Analysis on all pairwise comparisons to calculate the required information size (ie, the number of participants needed in a meta-analysis to detect or reject a certain intervention effect) and the cumulative Z-curve’s breach of relevant trial sequential monitoring boundaries.5253 67,73 A more detailed description of Trial Sequential Analysis can be found in the Trial Sequential Analysis manual52 and at http://www.ctu.dk/tsa/. For dichotomous outcomes, we will estimate the required information size based on the observed proportion of patients with an outcome in the control group (the cumulative proportion of patients with an event in the control groups relative to all patients in the control groups), a RR reduction or increase of 25%, an alpha of 5% for all outcomes, a beta of 10% and the observed diversity as suggested by the trials in the meta-analysis.

sec.title: Subgroup analyses and integration of heterogeneity
Subgroup analyses
sec.p: We will perform the following subgroup analyses when analysing the primary outcome (all-cause mortality).

list-item.p: Subgroup analyses of each patient group (eg, type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity, hypertension, chronic kidney disease).
Subgroup analyses of trials at high risk of bias compared with trials at low risk of bias.
Subgroup analyses of different doses of semaglutide, tirzepatide, CagriSema and liraglutide after dose escalation (at or above the median compared with below the median).
Subgroup analyses of different lengths of intervention (at or above the median compared with below the median).
Subgroup analyses of trials at risk of for-profit bias compared with trials without for-profit bias.
Subgroup analyses of patients at high risk of cardiovascular events (as defined by trialists) compared with those not explicitly defined at high risk of cardiovascular events.
Subgroup analyses based on different outcome definitions for each outcome.

sec.p: We will use the formal test for subgroup interactions in Stata.51 We will perform relevant unanticipated subgroup analyses, if we identify these.

sec.title: Sensitivity analyses
sec.p: To assess the potential impact of the missing data for dichotomous outcomes, we will perform the two following sensitivity analyses on all primary and secondary dichotomous outcomes.

list-item.p: ‘Best-worst-case’ scenario: We will assume that all participants lost to follow-up in the experimental group survived, had no myocardial infarction, had no stroke and were not hospitalised, and that all those participants lost to follow-up in the control group did not survive, had a myocardial infarction, had a stroke and were hospitalised.

‘Worst-best-case’ scenario: We will assume that all participants lost to follow-up in the experimental group did not survive, had a myocardial infarction, had a stroke and were hospitalised, and that all those participants lost to follow-up in the control group survived, had no myocardial infarction, had no stroke and were not hospitalised.

sec.p: We will present the results of both scenarios in our review. We will conduct sensitivity analyses using alternative definitions for each outcome and across different patient groups to assess the robustness of our findings. In addition, we will repeat all meta-analyses using ORs as effect measures. When time-to-event HRs are available, we will pool these results and conduct meta-analyses as sensitivity analyses. Any discrepancies between results will be reported. Other post hoc sensitivity analyses might be warranted if unexpected clinical or statistical heterogeneity is identified during the analysis of the review results.64

sec.title: Summary of findings table
sec.p: We will create a summary of findings table, including each of the prespecified outcomes. We will use the five Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluations (GRADE) considerations (bias risk of the trials, consistency of effect, imprecision, indirectness and publication bias) and the Confidence in Network Meta-Analysis approach to assess the certainty of the body of evidence.6474,78 We will assess imprecision using Trial Sequential Analysis by downgrading three levels if the accrued sample is <33% of diversity-adjusted required information size (DARIS); two levels if between 33% and 66% of DARIS; one level if >66% of DARIS and no downgrade if the cumulative Z-curve crosses the boundary for benefit, futility or harm.52 We will justify all decisions to downgrade the certainty of the evidence using footnotes, and we will make comments to aid the reader’s understanding of the review where necessary. First, we will present our results in the summary of findings table based on the results from the trials at overall low risk of bias, and second, we will present the results based on all trials.

sec.title: Network meta-analysis
sec.p: We will obtain information about the interventions of interest either from head-to-head trials or from trials comparing an experimental intervention with placebo, no intervention or ‘active placebo’. Hence, the synthesis comparator set consists of all the interventions listed in the background section as well as placebo, no intervention or ‘active placebo’ trials.

Descriptive statistics will also be generated for each treatment comparison, describing important clinical and methodological characteristics (eg, publication year, participant age). Each outcome dataset will be presented in a different network diagram, where the size of the nodes will be proportional to the total number of randomised participants, and the width of each edge will be weighted according to the number of studies comparing the connected treatments. We will additionally plot the edges of each network according to the average risk of bias per treatment comparison, using green for low, yellow for moderate and red for high risk of bias.
We will group all doses and administration forms of the same intervention into one node (eg, subcutaneous tirzepatide of 5, 10 and 15 mg will be grouped into one node).43 79

We hypothesise that any participant who meets inclusion criteria is, in principle, equally likely to be randomised to any of the interventions in the synthesis comparator set. Network meta-analysis will be performed using Stata 18 under frequentist framework51 (command: mvmeta).80 The network meta-analysis synthesises evidence for the comparative effectiveness of more than two alternative interventions for the same condition.81 We will only perform network meta-analysis if a connected network of trials can be conducted. If network meta-analysis is performed, we will, before conducting the network meta-analysis, assess two major assumptions: transitivity and consistency. We will then perform the statistical analysis in five steps. The first step is to draw a network geometry to overview the network relationship. The second step is to assess for the transitivity assumption across treatment comparisons in the network using boxplots and using meta-regression for effect modifiers (age and BMI), as well as evaluate the assumption of consistency using the design-by-treatment interaction model as a global test and node-splitting model of Dias et al.81,83 The third step is to make the network forest plot or interval plot in order to illustrate the summary effect size of the comparative effectiveness among interventions. The fourth step is to calculate cumulative rankings for identifying a superiority among interventions. This will only be done if one or more of the assessed GLP-1 RAs shows superiority in meta-analyses. The last step is to evaluate publication bias or effect modifiers for a valid inference from results. Potential effect modifiers will be the same as the subgroup analyses, for example, for-profit bias, type of comparator, age and BMI. We will also explore these through network subgroup meta-analyses.

The estimation of each treatment comparison will be reported separately using the relevant effect size (RR or mean difference (MD) or standardised mean difference (SMD)), a 95% CI and a 95% prediction interval. If two or more of the assessed interventions show superiority in meta-analyses, we will, along with the estimated effect sizes, present the ranking probabilities for each treatment being at each possible rank, as well as the surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA) or relevant P scores.84 85 A rank-heat plot will be used to depict the SUCRA values or P scores across all outcomes.86

sec.title: Patient and public involvement
sec.p: Patients and/or the public were not involved in the design, or conduct, or reporting, or dissemination plans of our research.

sec.title: Ethics and dissemination
sec.p: This systematic review does not require ethical approval and informed consent, as it does not use identifiable patient data. Findings of this systematic review will be published in international peer-reviewed scientific journals.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This systematic review with aggregate data meta-analyses, Trial Sequential Analysis and network meta-analysis aims to assess the effects of semaglutide, tirzepatide, CagriSema and liraglutide vs placebo—which may not be disease-specific—on hard binary outcomes for all assessed trial populations at increased risk of cardiovascular events. The primary outcome will be all-cause mortality. The secondary outcomes will be myocardial infarction, stroke and all-cause hospitalisation.

This protocol has several strengths. The protocol is reported in accordance with the guideline in the PRISMA-P statement,41 42 and the predefined detailed methodology follows the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions,43 the eight-step assessment suggested by Jakobsen et al,64 Trial Sequential Analysis52 53 and GRADE assessments.74 Thus, this protocol considers both risks of design errors, random errors and systematic errors. Meta-analysing all participants at increased risk of cardiovascular events increases the statistical power.

The protocol also has limitations. Primarily, there is a risk of statistical heterogeneity due to the inclusion of different types of participants at increased risk of cardiovascular events. Additionally, we anticipate that many trials—except cardiovascular outcome trials—will primarily focus on the effects of semaglutide, tirzepatide, CagriSema and liraglutide on glycaemic control and weight loss rather than hard binary outcomes. Another limitation is that we include only aggregate data rather than individual patient data. Lastly, some trials may focus solely on the short-term effects of semaglutide, tirzepatide, CagriSema and liraglutide. Consequently, these trials are expected to have short treatment and follow-up periods, which may reduce the likelihood of observing clinical events.
GLP-1 RAs are increasingly used worldwide, and clinicians must select the most suitable drug for their patients. Thus, this review is of the utmost relevance.
